scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Su primer single, «Love Me Do», entró en las listas el 11 de octubre de 1962, días antes de la crisis de los misiles. En 1963 provocaron una histeria femenina sin precedentes, rompieron la deferencia de los cincuenta y, por un breve tiempo, el sistema de clases: una revolución hecha con una melodía, un flequillo y un «yeah yeah yeah». En abril de 1964 ocuparon los cinco primeros puestos de Billboard, dispararon la venta de singles y convirtieron Gran Bretaña en la «Isla Pop». Su ejemplo obligaba a componer material propio. En 1966 hay pausas súbitas dentro del impulso imparable de «Rain».

podcast.title: Exemption from National Service (1957)
podcast.body: Ringo Starr, born on July 7, 1940, was exempt from compulsory national service in Britain. This exemption, due to the end of the obligation in 1957 for those born after October 1, 1939, allowed him to focus on music. "And future Beatles Ringo Starr was born on July 7, 1940."

podcast.body: In 1996, Ringo Starr traveled to Japan to participate in an advertisement for a brand of applesauce. The anecdote suggests that "Ringo" reportedly means "applesauce" in Japanese. "In 1996, Ringo Star went to Japan to take part in an ad for a brand of applesauce. By applesauce, apparently that's what Ringo means in Japanese."

xref.title: Exemption from National Service (1957, 1960)
xref.body: The end of compulsory national service in Britain in 1957 (for those born after Oct 1, 1939) and its complete abolition in November 1960 meant that young men in bands like The Quarrymen were exempt from military service. This freedom allowed members like John Lennon (born October 1940) and Ringo Starr (born July 1940), and by implication, all four future Beatles, to continue pursuing music rather than being drafted. "And that meant that the young men in a new group called the Corrie men wouldn't have to worry about going into the army, so they kept at it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Exemption from National Service (1957, 1960)
xref.body: All four members of The Beatles managed to avoid compulsory national service in Britain, which ended in 1957 for those born on or after October 1, 1939, and was completely abolished in November 1960. John Lennon (born October 1940) and Ringo Starr (born July 1940) were specifically mentioned as being exempt. This allowed them and countless other young British men to dedicate their time to forming bands and playing music, directly contributing to the explosion of the British music scene and the British Invasion. "And in November 1960, when compulsory service ended all together, all four members of the Beatles managed to avoid going into the army."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: King Edward Hotel Frenzy (1964)
xref.body: Upon their arrival at the King Edward Hotel in downtown Toronto on September 6, 1964, a frenzy of fans greeted The Beatles, leading to Paul McCartney having his shirt torn and Ringo Starr being separated from John and George. Although police quickly restored order on the street, Beatlemania continued inside, where a 14-year-old girl was found hiding in the linen closet of their royal suite. "Paul would have a shirt torn open by a fan, wrangle with separated from John and George, but thankfully police were able to quickly restore order on the street and get the band into the hotel."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Ringo Starr's Worry Over Montreal Threats (1964)
xref.body: Ringo Starr expressed genuine worry about the death threats received during The Beatles' 1964 Montreal concerts. He recalled that some individuals targeted him "as an English Jew," despite him not being Jewish, noting that while threats were often taken "in stride," this particular incident, despite more police presence, was one of the few times he was truly concerned. "Some people decided to make an example of me as an English Jew. The one major fault is, I'm not Jewish. Threats we took in stride. I mean, suddenly there'd be a few more cops, but this was one of the few times I was really worried."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Northern Songs Becomes Publicly Traded (1965)
xref.body: Two years after its inception, Northern Songs became a publicly traded company. At this point, Ringo Starr and George Harrison received small stakes in the business, though they were reportedly unhappy with their share. "Two years later, Northern Songs became a publicly traded company. At this point, Ringo and George also got small stakes in the business."

xref.title: George Harrison on Ringo's Death Threat (1990)
xref.body: In 1990, George Harrison recounted a specific death threat against Ringo Starr during The Beatles' 1964 Montreal visit. He stated that a Montreal newspaper reported someone intended to kill Ringo, possibly because they disliked his nose or because he was perceived as "the most British of the Beatles." "A Montreal newspaper reported that somebody was going to kill Ringo because they didn't like his nose or something, because he was probably the most British of the Beatles."

xref.title: Sierra Tucson Rehab and Relapse (1994-1996)
xref.body: Gahan underwent a period in the expensive Sierra Tucson rehab center in Arizona, which also attempted to help Ringo Starr, Whitney Houston, and Tiger Woods. Upon returning to Los Angeles, he found his house ransacked. He then overdosed on heroin, checking into the Sunset Marquis Hotel where he attempted suicide by slashing his wrists. After waking in a psych ward, he still only desired to get high and tried to hang himself in the bathroom. "There was a stint in rehab, the very expensive Sierra Tucson and Arizona."

xref.title: "Now and Then" - AI-Assisted Song (2020s)
xref.body: The Beatles created a brand new song, "Now and Then," utilizing artificial intelligence technology. Film director Peter Jackson was able to isolate John Lennon's vocals from a "bad sounding 1978 cassette demo," allowing Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr to add new parts, alongside George Harrison's contributions from a 1995 session. "But then we can point to what the Beatles did with AI and the song Now and Then, using brand new technology. Film director Peter Jackson was able to isolate John's vocals from a bad sounding 1978 cassette demo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Biggest Impact on Rock and Roll Drums
xref.body: Ringo Starr is credited with having the biggest single impact on drumming in rock and roll history. When The Beatles burst into the mainstream in 1964, Ringo's distinctive persona, described as "fun and slightly odd-looking," drew many young people to the drums, making playing look enjoyable and accessible. "The biggest thing that ever happened to drums in rock and roll was Ringo Star."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of the Modern Drum Kit

xref.title: Drummer Zach Starkey
xref.body: Zach Starkey, son of Ringo Starr, secured a gig with The Who and has been their on-call drummer for live performances ever since. His godfather, Keith Moon, was also The Who's drummer. "He got a gig with The Who, which seems fitting, given his family history. And since then, he's been on call with them whenever the Who plays live."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Drumming Influences
xref.body: Taylor Hawkins' drumming style was heavily influenced by progressive rock drummers such as Neil Peart of Rush, Stewart Copeland of The Police, and Phil Collins during his time with Genesis. Other influences included Stephen Perkins of Jane's Addiction, Ringo Starr, and his hero, Roger Taylor of Queen. "His heroes were Neil Pirate of Rush, Stuart Copeland of the police, and Phil Collins when he was with Genesis."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Father's Discouragement and Early Bands
xref.body: His father, Ringo Starr, gave him only one drum lesson and attempted to discourage him from a career in show business, advising him to be a doctor or lawyer instead of a musician. Despite this, Zach first joined a garage band called The Next, then a reformed version of the Spencer Davis Group. "Dad gave him exactly one lesson before he tried to dissuade his son about getting into show business. Be a doctor, be a lawyer, don't be a musician. Yeah, that didn't work. First came a garage band called The Next. Then he ended up in a reformed version of the Spencer Davis group."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Godfather and First Drum Kit
xref.body: Zach Starkey, son of Ringo Starr and Maureen, received his first drum kit from his godfather, Keith Moon of The Who. "Just like dad, he plays drums. He got his first kit from Keith Moon of the Who, who was also his godfather."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Individual Members' Solo Careers
xref.body: Following The Beatles' decision to stop touring in 1966 and their eventual breakup, individual members — John Lennon, George Harrison, Paul McCartney, and Ringo Starr — all went on to play solo shows in Canada. "And while the group would never play Canada again, the country would still see individual members over the next few years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influential Kit Setup
xref.body: The Ludwig drum kit that Ringo Starr played on his Ed Sullivan debut in 1964 became a benchmark. Even today, a vast number of players continue to use a 4 or 5-piece kit that has changed very little from that iconic setup. "But in between that is a vast number of players who use a 4 or 5 piece kit that's barely changed from the Ludwig set that Ringo played on Ed Sullivan in 1964."

xref.title: Left-Handed on Right-Handed Kit
xref.body: Stuart Copeland is left-handed but plays a drum kit set up for right-handers, which made his complex rhythms even more distinctive. This playing style has been compared to Ringo Starr, who, despite playing right-handed, frequently led with his left hand for fills and flourishes. As a three-piece band, The Police's structure provided ample space for Stuart Copeland's elaborate drumming. "His rhythms were made all the more complicated because Stuart is left-handed."

xref.title: Pioneer of the Matched Grip
xref.body: Ringo Starr significantly influenced new drummers by popularizing the "matched grip" for holding drum sticks. Traditionally, drummers used the "jazz grip," with one stick held like a club and the other from underneath with the palm facing upward. Ringo favored holding both sticks like clubs, allowing drummers to "attack their instrument" with more energy and a primal feel. His appearances on Ed Sullivan and in movies during the mid-1960s led almost every subsequent rock drummer to adopt the matched grip. "Ringo favorite the matched grip, where both sticks were held like clubs."

xref.title: Ringo Starr's Gregarious Nature
xref.body: Bob Burns, the CJAYTV reporter who announced The Beatles' arrival in Winnipeg and interviewed John Lennon, later stated that Ringo Starr was the most gregarious member of the band and appeared to be the most mature. "He would later state that Ringo Star was the most gregarious of the band and seemed the most mature."

xref.title: Ringo Starr's White Album (0000001) Sale
xref.body: Ringo Starr owned the unique copy of _The White Album_ bearing the serial number 0000001. He sold this highly sought-after collectible for charity in 2015, fetching $790,000. "It was Ringo Star who had number 00001. And he sold it off for charity in 2015 for $790,000."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Session Vocalist for Major Artists
xref.body: Mary Clayton has appeared on plenty of other legendary recordings as a session vocalist, lending her voice to tracks by artists such as Leonard Skynyrd ("Sweet Home Alabama"), Joe Cocker ("Feeling All Right"), Tori Amos, Coldplay, and Ringo Starr. Her extensive work demonstrates her reputation as a highly sought-after backup singer across various genres. "Mary has also appeared on plenty of other legendary recordings, Sweet Home Alabama by Leonard Skinnerd, Feeling All Right by Joe Cocker. Tori Amos, Coldplay, Ringo Star."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Signature Ludwig Kit
xref.body: Ringo Starr played a standard four-piece Ludwig drum kit, notable for its oyster gray finish. This particular setup, consisting of a snare, bass drum, mounted tom, and floor tom, became an influential template for many drummers. "He played a standard four-piece Ludwig kit with an oyster gray finish."

xref.title: Undeserved "Average Drummer" Reputation
xref.body: Ringo Starr has often been unfairly maligned with a "bad rap" as an average drummer and a below-average musician. However, drummers who have meticulously studied The Beatles' music recognize him as an innovative and tasteful player, refuting these accusations as both unfair and incorrect. "Ringo got this bad rap of not only being an average drummer, but also being a below-average musician."
